narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 68.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That high failure risk, not a judgment that you cannot succeed, is what triggered the rejection. Among the factors driving that estimate, your first-year class-rank decile was the most influential; at 4, below the accepted-student average of 6, it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor; at 35, below the accepted-student average of 37.18, it also pushed toward failure. Your third-year class-rank decile was the third most influential factor; at 5, slightly below the accepted-student average of 5.79, it pushed toward passing and partly offset the other two, but not enough to change the overall result. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction. Next, ask admissions whether you can submit an explanation or request reconsideration, and speak with a prelaw advisor about concrete steps to reduce bar-exam risk—such as retaking the LSAT if permitted, strengthening academic support, documenting improvement in later coursework, or delaying law school until your preparation is stronger.
